pageCache.pageTitle: Head’s Welcome | South Wilts Grammar School, Stratford Road, Salisbury, Wiltshire, SP1 3JJ
pageCache.text:
Head’s Welcome
Welcome to South Wilts Grammar School where excellence, curiosity and aspiration combine to form an exceptional educational experience and lead to remarkable outcomes and life opportunities for our students. Academic outcomes are exceptional at South Wilts, thanks to a curriculum that is broad, balanced and incredibly ambitious. We place high value on the vast range of subjects on offer throughout the school including in our vibrant sixth form where students choose from 25 A-level qualifications alongside several other level 3 options such as Sports Leaders Award and Arts Award. Our passion for education and providing opportunities for students enables them to follow their passions and prepare confidently for the future.
But academic success is not our only ambition. We strive to cultivate independent, resilient and responsible learners; young people who are ready not only for university or advanced study, but for life. Our most recent Ofsted inspection in January 2025 describes how “pupils are exceptionally proud to belong to this welcoming and vibrant school”, that the behaviour of students is “exemplary” and that “The school’s work to develop pupils’ character and understanding of the world is remarkable”.
Outside the classroom, our students engage in a rich tapestry of activities: music and sports, clubs and societies, international links and leadership roles. Relationships are warm and trusting and our entire philosophy is underpinned by our core values of kindness, involvement and aspiration. Additionally our two “golden threads” of sustainability as well as equality, diversity and inclusion are central to our way of life in the South Wilts community.
We believe that every student has enormous potential and our staff work tirelessly to ensure that potential is fulfilled in a supportive, friendly and dynamic environment. Whether you are joining us for Year 7 or entering our sixth form, you will find yourself at the heart of a school that prides itself on its strong culture of learning, mutual respect and ambition.
I warmly invite you to explore our website, contact us with any questions, and come and experience what makes our school so special.
Dr Amanda SmithHeadteacher

pageCache.pageTitle: Drama | South Wilts Grammar School, Stratford Road, Salisbury, Wiltshire, SP1 3JJ
pageCache.text:
Drama
Key Stage 3
Topics covered at Year 7 include:
Unit 1: Introduction to Drama
Unit 2: History of Theatre – Commedia D’ell Arte and Pantomime
Unit 3: Evaluating Live Theatre and Scripted Work – Treasure Island by Bryony Lavery
Unit 1: Devising a piece of Social Theatre – WW2 Evacuees
Unit 2: Scripted Work – Lord of the Flies Adapted by Nigel Williams
Unit 3: History of Theatre – Time Travel Through Theatre
Unit 1: Scripted Work – DNA by Dennis Kelly
Unit 2: Devising – Exploring a Range of GCSE Style Stimulus
Unit 3: Theatre in Education – The Power of Drama as a Social Tool
GCSE
Across the GCSE course, students will prepare for three assessed units:
In Year 10, students will begin their exploration of their set text for the written exam, Missing Dan Nolan, by Mark Wheeller, and will develop their skills in live theatre evaluation through two visits to the theatre. They will complete a mock of the devising exam, experiencing the full process of creating a piece of theatre from scratch – responding to an exam board stimulus, conducting research, developing their artistic intentions, purposefully using a range of rehearsal techniques, experimenting with different dramatic techniques to communicate meaning, reflecting on their work in progress and evaluating the final performance and their own application of skills as performers or designers. In the summer term of Year 10, students will also complete a mock of the scripted practical exam, using their set text from the written paper to choose extracts from to bring to life as performers and designers. Not only will this give them invaluable experience in stage craft and the challenges of bringing a scripted extract to life, it will also give them first-hand experience of the practical realisation of their examined set text, equipping them with vital knowledge, key skills and examples they can apply in the final written exam.
In Year 11, students will prepare to complete their real devising exam in December and will work on their written coursework accompanying this throughout. There will be a further two theatre trips of contrasting genres and styles to help students continue to develop their skills in analysing and evaluating a wide range of theatre, to allow them to confidently tackle the Live Theatre paper in the written exam. Across the year, students will revise their set text for the written exam, Missing Dan Nolan, and will continue to develop their exam technique ahead of the final written paper in May. Their practical experience of the course will culminate in their real scripted exam, in which they will have a choice of suitable plays to bring extracts to life from as designers or performers. This will be worked on throughout January to April/May and will be assessed externally by a visiting examiner.
A Level
For information about A Level Theatre Studies, please visit our Sixth Form Subjects page.
Extra Curricular
In addition to regular trips to the theatre for exam classes, we run as much extra-curricular Drama as we can to provide students with a wealth of different experiences and opportunities within our subject, which is so important in nurturing vital interdisciplinary skills – such as teamwork, communication, problem solving, critical thinking, time management, creativity – and building resilience.

pageCache.text:
Computer Science
Key Stage 3
Over the course of three years students gain a wealth of knowledge in using many computer programs which will equip them well for any job they wish to take on in the future. They will learn how to use ‘office applications’, develop skills in digital literacy, as well as the fundamentals of logical thinking and problem solving through programming and the principles of computer systems.

Data Representation (binary, images, and sound)
Logic gates
Computer Networks (wired and wireless)
Data Encryption and Cryptology
Programming in Python
Working collaboratively online using Office 365

How the internet works.
How Operating systems work
Programming in Python
Key Stage 4 (GCSE)
Computer Science is an ideal course for those who want to develop their problem solving and logic skills. It will also appeal to students who are practical and like to create. Students who are curious about digital technology are also very well suited to this course.
Lessons are split between the delivery of paper 2 course content (such as data representation, computer systems, computer networks, network security), lessons on the theoretical concepts of paper 1 (data structures, designing programs, and key algorithms) as well as practical programming lessons.
Year 11 will see the completion of the full GCSE. We will cover the remainder of the theory topics for the paper 2, such as databases and the legal and ethical issues in computer science. Students will complete a thorough programme of revision including past papers, defining key concepts, exam techniques and how to respond to programming exam paper questions.
Assessment is through two written theory exams (2 hours, and 1.75 hours respectively) containing short and medium-length answer questions.

pageCache.pageTitle: French | South Wilts Grammar School, Stratford Road, Salisbury, Wiltshire, SP1 3JJ
pageCache.text:
French
Key Stage 3
During Year 7 students cover the basics of French grammar and pronunciation in a variety of contexts. Topics covered include: personal details, family and pets and school as well as phrases to use in a French town. Students are introduced to the notion of noun, gender and regular and irregular verb forms. Students are also introduced to the basic skills of speaking, listening, reading and writing.
In Year 8, French students build on the work begun in Year 7. They continue to develop their listening, reading, speaking and writing skills. New grammar topics include using the irregular verbs aller and faire, and we consolidate the use of regular -er verbs and adjective agreemens. The topics are At Home and Daily Life, in a French Town and Free Time. We continue to work on pronunciation and confidence with speaking.
In Year 9, French students build on Year 7 and 8 work. They continue to develop their listening, reading, speaking and writing skills. New grammar topics include using two verbs together, including modal verbs and using aller + the infinitve to refer to future events, as well as an introduction to the past tense. The topics are Going out, Food and Drink, Recent Events, Health and Healthy Lifestyles, Music, TV and Film and Holidays. We continue to work on pronunciation and confidence with speaking.
Key Stage 4 (GCSE)
The French course in Year 10 and 11 is a continuation of the work done in the previous years. The main aim of the course is to allow students to develop the ability to use French as a means of practical communication. A competent, accurate use of grammar is also important. The language used is as authentic and useful as possible, dealing with the topics of People and Lifestyle, Popular Culture and Communication and the World Around us.
Four main skills are developed, understanding the written and spoken language and communicating in the written and spoken language. All four skills (listening, reading, writing and speaking) are assessed with an equal 25% weighting, at the end of Year 11.
During the lessons, students are expected to participate as actively as possible. There is plenty of listening and reading comprehension practice, and students learn grammar and writing skills. We also aim to help our students to become confident speakers of French who truly enjoy communicating in the language. There is a trip to France in Year 10.
Key Stage 5 (A Level)
For information about A Level French at SWGS, please visit our Sixth Form Subjects page.

pageCache.pageTitle: Art | South Wilts Grammar School, Stratford Road, Salisbury, Wiltshire, SP1 3JJ
pageCache.text:
Art
Year 7
Year 7 Art starts by teaching and learning the foundation drawing skills. Students produce a Still life drawing based on simple shaped objects utilising the elements line, tone, proportion, scale and composition. Colour theory is then introduced and students learn how to mix paint/colours to create a colour wheel. The skill of mixing colours and then applying paint is used to produce a cool/warm colours tree composition. Key Artists related to the understanding of colour theory are introduced and investigated.
This unit builds on students’ realistic drawing skills but introduces concept of Abstraction inspired by the Artist Chuck Close. Students are able to achieve an accurate likeness of a Self Portrait by using the grid method and they explore other drawing/rendering techniques modelled in the work of famous Artists’ Portraiture. Students can take inspiration for the background of their portrait from Artists Kehinde Wiley, Chuck Close or a particular cultural patterned background that is pertinent to their heritage.
Plants are the subject matter for students to explore the formal elements of line and shape to create a pattern based on a simple poly board design using the reduction method printing process. Students are informed by the work of Henri Rousseau’s Jungle paintings, Matisse’s Abstract leaf ’Cut Outs’, William Morris’s print designs and other contemporary print designers.
Year 8
Students will use Pop Art as the inspiration for pieces of Artwork in this project. They will explore Lichtenstein’s drawing techniques, Warhol’s mass-produced iconic products and create a collage in the style of Richard Hamilton. The students’ final outcome will be an acrylic painting informed and inspired by the work of 2 contemporary Artists whose artwork features bold, bright products and packaging of ‘Life Today’.
‘What is a Landscape?’ is the starting point for this project. Students are introduced to the history of the Landscape and explore the way that the Impressionists, post-Impressionists and Expressionists have tackled this genre with tasks employing different mark making techniques. Students are then given the task of creating a clay tile based on a landscape and including the mark making skills they have acquired.
Students explore the patterns and symbols used in the Artwork of different cultures from around the world. The working methods and practices of artists related to specific cultures; Islamic, African and Japanese, are investigated and responded to using a range of media and techniques. The outcome for this project is a decorative Islamic style tile design.
Year 9
Students carry out a small scale project in the same format as those at GCSE working independently to record, experiment and develop work to a personal outcome. The current theme is ‘Identity’ and the students will produce artwork that investigates; related Artists’ work, drawing/painting styles and planning for a final piece. For this project the final outcome will take the form of an ‘Identity Quilt’.
Students are introduced to and investigate the pioneers of the Modern Art movement. They learn about the Artists’ styles and techniques and acquire the practical skills to apply the various techniques. Each student presents their research in the form of a Modern Art Movement Timeline booklet.
Students carry out an in depth personal written study on a Modern or Contemporary Artist, acquiring art historical knowledge and visual culture skills. Their chosen Artist is then used as inspiration to create a final outcome/cover to their book.

Key Stage 4 (GCSE)
Students follow the AQA specifications for English Language and English Literature. In English Language, Year 10 begins with the Journeys and Transformations unit, which develops the skills required for Language Paper 1 while taking students well beyond the demands of the examination, exploring genre and thematic ideas through writing and debate. Through a range of fiction extracts, students refine their analytical and evaluative skills, exploring how genre shapes meaning, style and structure. They apply this understanding to their own fiction writing, crafting original pieces for different audiences and purposes by drawing on the conventions of genres they have encountered. Students complete a Spoken Language presentation, for which they receive separate accreditation.
In English Literature, students begin their study of the GCSE texts, all of which are connected through the broad themes of power and conflict. They start with Shakespeare’s Macbeth, exploring ideas of tyranny and corruption within the tragic genre, developing their understanding of Shakespeare’s methods and dramatic conventions. Students then move on to Animal Farm, as they consider themes such as hierarchy, rebellion and complicity, while refining their knowledge of satire from Year 9. Towards the end of Year 10, students begin both the seen and unseen poetry units, exploring diverse representations of power and conflict in heritage and contemporary poetry ranging from 1798 to the twenty-first century.
In English Language, students study the Advocacy and Adversity unit, which prepares them for Language Paper 2 through thematically linked contemporary and historical non-fiction texts, developing their comparative analytical skills. Building on their understanding of purpose, audience and form, students develop an appreciation of voice and style in both their own and others’ writing.
In English Literature, students continue their poetry studies, further developing their understanding of both anthology and unseen poetry. Students then study their final GCSE text, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, exploring themes of personal power and inner conflict within the context of a Gothic Victorian novella. Throughout the year, students draw connections across all four GCSE literature components through the overarching theme of power and conflict.
Extensive revision and consolidation units then help students refine their knowledge, strengthen examination skills and prepare thoroughly for the series of GCSE examinations in both subjects.

pageCache.pageTitle: Geography | South Wilts Grammar School, Stratford Road, Salisbury, Wiltshire, SP1 3JJ
pageCache.text:
Geography
Key Stage 3
The Year 7 curriculum aims to get students familiar with their local area and teach them the foundation disciplinary skills required to be a successful geographer.
Autumn Term – Year 7 geography begins with a topic focused on the subject’s fundamentals. Locational and place knowledge, physical, human and environmental geography and fieldwork are all a focus. This topic aims to have students ready for what the rest of KS3 geography will offer. Secondly, students learn the vital map skills of 6 figure grid references, measuring distance, identifying OS symbols, contours and describing a route. Students then investigate global climate zones. The aim of this topic is to apply some of the knowledge likely developed at primary school to a wider variety of global climate zones. Examples include the tropical rainforest, hot deserts and tundra.
Spring Term – Students turn their attention to some human geography and the demographics of the United Kingdom. Here they will study how our population has changed, focusing on place examples such as Leicester and Salisbury.
Summer Term – This term begins with a topic on coastal landscapes. This illustrates how rapidly our coastlines are changing and the factors responsible for it. A visit to Lulworth Cove, Durdle Door and Stair Hole will form the basis of a fieldwork investigation. The academic year is concluded by a study of our changing climate. This topic will allow students to analyse the science behind climate change whilst considering some of the mitigation and adaptation strategies being adopted.
The Year 8 course builds on the substantive and disciplinary knowledge gained in year 7, with a stronger focus on places and the issues they are trying to manage.
Autumn Term – Students study the location of European countries, capital cities and main physical features. They then learn about the EU and our changing relationship with it. Students will follow this by investigating the geography of food, looking at why countries have varying access to food. They will learn about Fairtrade, focused on the pros and cons of the idea and label.
Spring Term –Students will study the topic of amazing places which will involve assessing the management of fragile ecosystems like The Great Barrier Reef and Savannah. Additionally, students will discover more about the cold environment of Antarctica and its complicated political landscape.
Summer Term – The topic of Tourism will be studied, and students will then be given the opportunity to design their own UK based or global tourist destination based on what they have learnt. Here students will be required to focus on the more sustainable elements of tourism and how they can be more widely implemented.
The major theme of this year is global issues and the substantive and disciplinary knowledge needed to succeed at GCSE, if geography is an option being considered.
Autumn Term – Students will study the exciting topic of our violent planet – looking at why tectonic activity occurs and what we can do to minimise the impact. They study events from the past and present before students move on to consider the challenge of atmospheric hazards. This topic is essential for any student planning to study geography at GCSE.
Spring Term – Plastic pollution in our oceans, deforestation of fragile forest ecosystems and our changing climate are all pressing global issues. In this topic students will explore the causes and assess the management attempts aimed at preventing them. Students will follow this up with the start to a big topic focused on human geography. Economic development is up first with a focus on how we measure the development, as well as the causes of our current global development gap.
Summer Term – Students continue their work on human geography by learning about national and global patterns of migration. What causes migration in contrasting places and what the varying impacts of migration can be. Students will conclude the year with a short place study of the dynamic continent of Africa. Here students will explore the significant climate zones and diverse human worlds.
GCSE
GCSE geography will inspire, motivate and challenge you. Geography will develop you as an effective and independent learner and you will become a critical and reflective thinker with an ever increasing mind. Throughout the two years you will develop your knowledge and understanding of geographical concepts and our changing world.
Paper 1: Living with the physical environment (88 marks, 1 hour 30 minutes and 35% of GCSE Qualification):
Section A: The challenge of natural hazards (33 marks) Section B: The living world (25 marks) Section C: Physical landscapes in the UK (30 marks)
Paper 2: Challenges in the human environment (88 marks, 1 hour 30 minutes and 35% of GCSE Qualification):
Section A: Urban issues and challenges (33 marks) Section B: The changing economic world (30 marks) Section C: The challenge of resource management (25 marks)
Paper 3: Geographical applications (76 marks, 1 hour 15 minutes and 30% of GCSE Qualification):
Section A: Issue evaluation (37 marks) Section B: Fieldwork (39 marks)

pageCache.pageTitle: German | South Wilts Grammar School, Stratford Road, Salisbury, Wiltshire, SP1 3JJ
pageCache.text:
German
Key Stage 3
During Year 7 students cover the basics of German grammar and pronunciation in a variety of contexts. Topics covered include: personal details, family and pets and school. Students are introduced to the notion of noun, gender and regular and irregular verb forms as well as some of the intricacies of German sentence order. Students are also introduced to the basic skills of speaking, listening, reading and writing.
In Year 8, German students build on the work begun in Year 7. They continue to develop their listening, reading, speaking and writing skills. Grammar topics include the present tense, using gern, possessive adjectives, and using es gibt. The topics are Free Time, At Home and In a German Town. We continue to work on pronunciation and confidence with speaking.
In Year 9, German students build on the work begun in Year 8. They continue to develop their listening, reading, speaking and writing skills. New grammar topics include subordinating conjunctions, an introduction to the future and past tenses and modal verbs. Other grammar points are comparatives and superlatives and ‘verb-comma-verb’ constructions. The topics are Music, Health and Food and Drink, School and Future Plans, A Holiday in the Past and Going Out. We continue to work on pronunciation and confidence with speaking.
GCSE
The German course in Year 10 and 11 is a continuation of the work done in the previous years. The main aim of the course is to allow students to develop the ability to use German as a means of practical communication. A competent, accurate use of grammar is also important. The language used is as authentic and useful as possible, dealing with the topics of People and Lifestyle, Popular Culture and Communication and the World Around us.
Four main skills are developed, understanding the written and spoken language and communicating in the written and spoken language. All four skills (listening, reading, writing and speaking) are assessed with an equal 25% weighting, at the end of Year 11.
During the lessons, students are expected to participate as actively as possible. There is plenty of listening and reading comprehension practice, and students learn grammar and writing skills. We also aim to help our students to become confident speakers of German who truly enjoy communicating in the language.
